tldr: By reconstructing hand motions from monocular human videos and porting them into a simulator as a "tactile completion engine," this work demonstrates zero-shot transfer of visual-tactile dexterous manipulation policies without any robot-side data collection.
hero_caption: Overview of Dex-X. Hand motions and object relationships are reconstructed from monocular human videos, and physical interactions are recreated inside a simulator to complete missing force and tactile data. The resulting visual-tactile policy transfers zero-shot to real-world grasping and tool-use tasks without any real-robot fine-tuning.
overview:
Videos of humans using tools and grasping objects with their hands are abundant on the web, making them an attractive data source for learning dexterous manipulation. However, videos lack a crucial piece of information: tactile sensing (contact forces). Tactile feedback is essential for holding tools securely and maintaining contact during tasks, yet force cannot be directly read from video frames.

To address this, the authors had the insight to use a physics simulator as a tactile completion engine. They reconstruct 3D trajectories of the hand and object from monocular video, retarget them to the robot's kinematics, and recreate the physical interaction inside a simulator. Using the force and tactile feedback provided by the simulator's contact dynamics, they train a policy via reinforcement learning (RL), which is then distilled into a deployable student policy operating on point clouds and fingertip tactile sensors available on the real robot.

For real-world evaluation, they used a 29-DoF dexterous hand-arm platform (Franka FR3 + Sharpa HA4) and tested zero-shot transfer without any fine-tuning in the real environment. The policy achieved a 93% (28/30) success rate on cube picking and 53% (16/30) on a squeegee table-cleaning task involving continuous contact. Furthermore, they observed zero-shot generalization to unseen object geometries, demonstrating that simulation can serve as an effective bridge between passive video demonstrations and real-world dexterous manipulation.
contributions: Proposed Dex-X, a framework that replays motion trajectories extracted from monocular human videos in a physics simulator to serve as a "tactile completion engine" that recovers missing contact forces.

Constructed a training paradigm where a privileged state-based teacher policy is trained via reinforcement learning using simulator tactile information, then distilled into a student policy operating on deployable point-cloud and fingertip tactile inputs.
Demonstrated zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and generalization to unseen object geometries across grasping and tool-use tasks on a 29-DoF dexterous hand-arm platform without additional fine-tuning.

sections.heading: Human videos lack touch: Completing physics with simulation
sections.summary: While human videos are rich in dexterous manipulation skills, they lack tactile information such as contact forces, making direct use for robot contact tasks difficult. Dex-X leverages simulation as a tactile completion engine, combining video-derived motion references with tactile-aware reinforcement learning to achieve zero-shot transfer to real hardware.
sections.details:
Dexterous manipulation—coordinating a high-DoF arm and multi-fingered hand under complex contact dynamics—has long been a major challenge in robotics. While recent advances in reinforcement learning and imitation learning have demonstrated impressive skills, they typically demand extensive trial-and-error in painstakingly built simulators or real-robot data collection with specialized teleoperation setups and sensing gloves, making scaling difficult.

Turning to the vast library of human manipulation videos on the web is an appealing alternative, but it faces two major hurdles. First, videos contain no tactile information such as contact forces, making it hard to learn stable grasping and contact-maintaining control. Second, transferring policies from simulation to the real world suffers from perception noise and contact model mismatches (the sim-to-real gap).

Dex-X addresses these challenges by framing simulation as a "tactile completion engine." By reconstructing 3D trajectories of the hand and object from video and allowing them to interact physically in simulation, it synthesizes contact force signals that are absent in the original video. These signals supervise reinforcement learning, and the resulting policy is distilled into a deployable model that takes point clouds, proprioception (joint states), and fingertip tactile sensing as inputs. Without any real-world data collection or fine-tuning, Dex-X achieves a 93% success rate on cube picking and 53% on squeegee table cleaning.

sections.heading: At the crossroads of video learning, sim-to-real, and visual-tactile manipulation
sections.summary: This work bridges three research directions: generating robot motions from human videos, sim-to-real reinforcement learning, and integrated visual-tactile control. Dex-X stands out by fusing video-derived motion priors with simulated force generation to enable zero-shot transfer of autonomous visual-tactile policies.
sections.details:
This research builds upon three main bodies of prior work:

- **Dexterous manipulation from human demonstrations**: To bridge the embodiment gap between human hands and robot manipulators, prior methods have explored motion retargeting, trajectory optimization, and contact-consistent reconstruction. Dex-X complements these techniques by using retargeted motions to guide reinforcement learning while generating force-level tactile supervision in simulation, yielding a policy that performs closed-loop control using real tactile sensors at deployment.

- **Sim-to-real transfer for dexterous manipulation**: Large-scale simulation RL and domain randomization have enabled multi-fingered in-hand manipulation, grasping, and tool use. However, handling contact dynamics mismatches and actuator delays remains difficult. Dex-X narrows the RL exploration space using video-based motion priors and uses force-mediated learning to achieve robust transfer.

- **Visual-tactile manipulation**: Tactile feedback provides critical contact information that is often occluded from vision alone. Prior works such as Robot Synesthesia have integrated tactile signals into point-cloud representations. Dex-X takes this concept further by synthesizing force-level tactile feedback from video demonstrations through simulation, learning autonomous policies for tasks requiring sustained contact between the environment, tools, and objects.

sections.heading: A three-stage framework: Video recovery, privileged expert training, and student distillation
sections.summary: Dex-X proceeds through three stages: (1) hand-object trajectory reconstruction and retargeting from monocular video, (2) privileged state-based reinforcement learning leveraging simulated contact forces, and (3) distillation into a student policy conditioned on point clouds and tactile sensors.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
From a dataset of monocular human manipulation videos, the goal is to learn a visual-tactile policy $\pi(a_t \mid o_t, r_{t+1})$ capable of reproducing the demonstrated skill across varying initial conditions. The observation $o_t$ consists of proprioception, vision, and tactile sensing, conditioned on the next-step motion reference $r_{t+1}$. The core idea is completing the tactile information missing from videos through simulation.

### 3.2 Extracting Motion Priors and Spatial Augmentation
- **Hand and Object Motion Reconstruction**: FoundationPose estimates 6D object poses, WiLoR initializes hand poses, and optimization is performed using the MANO model with temporal smoothness and anti-penetration constraints at 30 Hz.
- **Retargeting to the Robot**: A two-stage optimization is applied. First, the arm tracks the wrist trajectory; second, the arm and hand are jointly optimized with higher weights placed on the thumb, index finger, and fingertip keypoints.
- **Spatial Augmentation**: To handle variations in initial positions and orientations, planar translations and yaw rotations ($\Delta\psi$) are applied as perturbations across entire demonstrations.

### 3.3 Training the Privileged State Expert
The privileged expert is trained in simulation using PPO with an Asymmetric Actor-Critic framework. The actor receives the robot state, the next-step motion reference, object BPS geometric features, noisy object poses, and five fingertip contact forces (scalars) from the simulator. The critic is given additional privileged information, including future target states and ground-truth object data. The reward function combines trajectory tracking, object tracking, contact shaping (approach and slip prevention), and task success rewards.

### 3.4 Policy Distillation and Sim-to-Real Transfer
The privileged expert is distilled via DAgger into a student policy that operates within the real robot's observation space. Instead of explicit object geometry, the student receives a contact point cloud combining scene points from depth images (1024 points), hand keypoints (6 points), and fingertip tactile points (25 points). Tactile points are augmented with their corresponding fingertip contact force scalar values, and features are extracted through a shared PointNet backbone. The real robot runs under 30 Hz closed-loop control.

captions.F2: The Dex-X training framework. On the left (Stage 1), a privileged state expert is trained with RL using target trajectories extracted from videos and contact forces from the simulator. On the right (Stage 2), the expert's behavior is distilled via DAgger into a deployable student policy that takes an integrated point-cloud representation (scene points + fingertip forces) through PointNet.

sections.heading: From simulation benchmarks to real-world zero-shot transfer and ablations
sections.summary: In simulation, Dex-X achieved a 65.9% average success rate across six task categories, substantially outperforming baselines. In real-world tests without fine-tuning, it reached a 93% success rate (28/30) on cube picking and 53% (16/30) on squeegee cleaning, proving that both tactile and visual modalities are essential for robust execution.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The real-world platform consists of a Franka FR3 arm and a Sharpa HA4 dexterous hand (29 DoF per arm), equipped with a fixed RealSense depth camera and fingertip tactile sensors. Tasks span six categories: lifting (cup, cube), tool use (squeegee, hammer), pin insertion, in-hand rotation, in-hand translation, and bimanual handover.

### 4.2 Q1: Dexterous Manipulation Learning in Simulation
In simulation, the Dex-X state expert achieved an average success rate of 65.9%, outperforming the imitation-learning-based ManipTrans (21.9%) and pure motion retargeting (5.2%). On a five-task single-arm benchmark, it also outperformed the RL baseline DAPG (61.7% vs. 40.6%). The margin was particularly pronounced on tasks requiring prolonged contact, such as tool use (74.3% vs. 35.0%) and in-hand translation (64.8% vs. 11.5%). While imitation learning often suffers from slippage during sustained contact, Dex-X learns force-feedback-driven adjustments through RL, maintaining stability.

### 4.3 Q2: Roles of Visual and Tactile Representations (Ablations)
- **Simulation**: The point-cloud + tactile student achieved a 58% success rate under relaxed criteria, but dropped to 45% when tactile inputs were removed. Comparing three tactile representations—scalar force, binary contact, and 3D force vectors—showed minimal performance differences, leading to the selection of scalar force for ease of matching real sensors.
- **Real-Robot Ablation**: On cube picking, the full visual-tactile policy succeeded in 28/30 trials (93%). Success dropped sharply to 14/30 without vision, 11/30 without touch, and 8/30 with proprioception alone, confirming that both modalities are vital for grasp initiation and contact maintenance.

### 4.4 Q3: Real-World Deployment and Generalization to Unseen Objects
In zero-shot real-world evaluations, Dex-X achieved 28/30 on cube picking, 24/30 on cup pouring, 22/30 on cup lifting, and 16/30 on squeegee cleaning. Squeegee cleaning is particularly challenging because it demands continuous contact while moving. Furthermore, the policy achieved 23/30 on an unseen thin rectangular prism, demonstrating zero-shot generalization across object shapes (though success dropped to 7–8/30 on square cubes and toy ducks, highlighting challenges with substantial geometric shifts).

captions.F3: Representative real-world visual-tactile dexterous manipulation tasks. From left to right: cube picking, squeegee table cleaning, hammer swinging, water pouring, and in-hand squeegee rotation, demonstrating the ability to maintain prolonged, stable contact.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Simulation bridges passive video and physical manipulation
sections.summary: Dex-X establishes a framework for learning dexterous manipulation from monocular human videos. By employing simulation as a tactile completion engine, it supplements motion references with force supervision, enabling zero-shot transfer and generalization to unseen geometries on real hardware.
sections.details:
This paper presented Dex-X, a framework for learning visual-tactile dexterous manipulation policies from monocular human videos. The core contribution lies in treating physics simulation as a "tactile completion engine" that synthesizes contact force feedback unobtainable from passive videos.

By uniting video-extracted motion references with tactile-aware reinforcement learning, the system achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a 29-DoF arm-hand platform without real-world fine-tuning. It demonstrates contact stability far superior to imitation learning baselines and generalizes to novel object shapes. These results suggest that physical completion through simulation is a promising bridge for scaling robot physical skill learning using web-scale human video datasets.

sections.heading: Remaining challenges: Long-horizon interactions and tactile resolution
sections.summary: Limitations remain in compounding perceptual and control errors during long-horizon tasks, as well as generalization across large shape and category variations. Additionally, current tactile representations are restricted to scalar fingertip forces, leaving richer signals like slip and shear for future work.
sections.details:
Several limitations remain in the proposed approach:

- **Long-horizon interactions and generalization bounds**: Policy performance degrades in the presence of perceptual noise, controller discrepancies, or drastic shifts in object shape and category. Furthermore, deployment still relies on retargeted motion references, requiring broader demonstration diversity and more flexible task-specification mechanisms.

- **Tactile resolution**: The current tactile representation is limited to 1D scalar forces per fingertip (5-dimensional total), leaving out richer information like pressure distributions, shear forces, micro-slips, and contact patch geometry. Incorporating higher-resolution tactile sensing could enable even finer contact adjustments.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details, sim-to-real force/trajectory analysis, and spatial augmentation
sections.summary: Details on spatial data augmentation, force profile and wrist trajectory error analysis during sim-to-real transfer, observation spaces and reward design for expert and student policies, and safety controls during real-robot deployment.
sections.details:
### Sim-to-Real Force and Trajectory Analysis (Appendix B)
Comparing contact force profiles across five fingers between simulation and reality revealed strong alignment in contact onset timing and force distribution patterns. The mean wrist trajectory tracking error was 2.83 cm (with trial-to-trial standard deviations between 0.46 and 0.82 cm), showing high reproducibility. Tracking discrepancies stemmed primarily from arm compliance under forward loads and initial object placement offsets (up to 1 cm), while the underlying quality of the learned motion was preserved.

### Spatial Augmentation and Retargeting (Appendix D)
To learn robust policies from a single demonstration video, spatial augmentations including planar translations ($\pm 5$ cm) and yaw rotations ($\pm 10^\circ$) were applied relative to the arm base (Figure F8). Infeasible retargeting samples with end-effector errors exceeding 8 cm were automatically discarded.

### Observation Spaces and Distillation Setup (Appendix E, I)
- **Privileged Expert**: Actor input is 557-dimensional (proprioception, motion reference, object BPS features, 5D fingertip forces, etc.), while the critic input is 705-dimensional, incorporating privileged ground-truth object states and future target states over 5 steps.
- **Student Policy**: For deployment, explicit object geometry is removed. The observation is 481-dimensional, consisting of a 417-dimensional vector observation combined with a 64-dimensional feature extracted via PointNet from 1055 points (1024 scene points + 6 hand keypoints + 25 tactile points) across 5 channels (3D coordinates + point type + force). DAgger distillation was conducted over 30 iterations with an annealing mixing coefficient.

### Control and Safety (Appendix J)
The control loop runs at 30 Hz (~33 ms). Depth acquisition (~5 ms), kinematics (~2 ms), inference (~3 ms), and ROS 2 communication (~1 ms) leave ample room for real-time processing. For real-robot safety, joint position/velocity limits, action delta limits, and two-stage reset trajectories are enforced.

captions.F8: Spatial augmentation applied prior to retargeting. Sampling planar position offsets ($\Delta X, \Delta Y$) and yaw perturbations (represented by color changes and arrow orientations) relative to the arm base generates diverse initial configurations from a single video demonstration.

takeaways: Synthesizing the primary missing component in video imitation learning—tactile sensing—via a physics simulator provides a powerful blueprint for scaling robot manipulation from web-scale video data.

A two-stage pipeline that first trains a privileged reinforcement learning expert before distilling it via DAgger into a point-cloud + tactile student is key to stable sim-to-real transfer on complex 29-DoF platforms.

Fingertip tactile sensing does not necessarily require expensive high-dimensional tactile arrays; 1D scalar force values per finger, combined with appropriate domain randomization, dramatically boost grasp and tool-use stability.
limitations: Deploying the trained policy still relies on a retargeted reference motion trajectory extracted from video, stopping short of fully autonomous, prompt-driven task generation.
Tactile sensing is simplified to normal scalar force values, leaving richer high-resolution feedback—such as slip detection, shear forces, and contact patch shapes—unexplored.
While the policy exhibits some zero-shot generalization across object shapes, success rates drop sharply when encountering severe geometric differences, such as toy ducks.
